pos: n. (a copper alloy; the metal of the outer court and of judgment; rendering Hebrew nechosheth, Greek chalkos)
etymology: From the Saxon braes. The Hebrew nechosheth more strictly denotes copper or bronze, the Authorized Version's brass covering the whole family of copper alloys; the same consonants give nachash, a serpent, and the pun is unmistakable in the brasen serpent Moses lifted up.
biblical_def: Brass in Scripture is the metal of the outer court and so of judgment borne. Gold belongs to the holy place, where God dwells; brass belongs to the altar and the laver, where sin is dealt with before a man may go further in — the arrangement is theological before it is architectural. The most striking use is the remedy in the wilderness: “And Moses made a serpent of brass, and put it upon a pole, and it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived” (Numbers 21:9), which our Lord makes the express type of his own lifting up. The judgment-metal is shaped into the very image of the curse, and the dying are healed by looking. Brass also figures the hardness of a heaven shut in judgment: “thy heaven that is over thy head shall be brass” (Deuteronomy 28:23), the covenant curse for disobedience. Paul uses it for religious noise without love — “I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal” (1 Corinthians 13:1) — the metal that resonates loudly and contains nothing. And John sees the glorified Christ with “feet like unto fine brass, as if they burned in a furnace” (Revelation 1:15), the Judge standing on the metal of judgment.
webster_summary: Copper alloy; in the tabernacle the metal of the outer court, the altar, and the laver — hence the metal of judgment borne. Moses' serpent of brass is the type of Christ lifted up.
webster_full: BRASS, n. [Sax. braes.] An alloy of copper and zinc, of a yellow color; in Scripture usually copper or bronze.
2. Impudence; a brazen face — a figurative use.
3. In the tabernacle, the metal of the altar of burnt offering, the laver, and the court vessels.
4. A figure of hardness or of a heaven shut up; as, thy heaven shall be brass, Deut. 28.
5. In Scripture, of the serpent lifted up in the wilderness, Num. 21; of the feet of the glorified Christ, Rev. 1.
corruption_summary: Tabernacle metals are read as decoration or as ancient technology, and their teaching is lost. Scripture assigns them by station — brass at the altar, gold in the holiest — and the assignment preaches the way of approach to God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The loss is one of typological literacy rather than doctrinal attack. A reader who takes the metals as furnishing detail will skim Exodus and Leviticus as inventory, when in fact the gradient from brass to gold as one moves from court to holy place to holiest is a diagram of atonement: judgment must be met at the brasen altar and cleansing at the brasen laver before there is any question of the golden furniture within.

The principle to recover is the one our Lord himself drew from this metal. As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up — and the type is exact at the point most people miss. The remedy was made in the form of the curse itself, a brass serpent for serpent-bitten men, just as he who knew no sin was made sin for us. The dying Israelite was not asked to fetch anything or do anything; he was asked to look. That is why 1 Corinthians 13:1 stings: brass can also be all sound and no substance, and a religion of noise without love has the metal without the meaning.
roots_summary: Hebrew nechosheth is copper or bronze, sharing consonants with nachash, serpent; nachush means brazen or hard. Greek chalkos is copper or brass, and chalkolibanon is the fine burnished brass of Revelation 1:15.
roots_lines: Hebrew nechosheth (H5178) — copper, bronze, brass; the metal of the altar and the laver.
Hebrew nachash (H5175) — serpent; the wordplay behind the brasen serpent of Numbers 21.
Hebrew nechushtan (H5180) — the name Hezekiah gave the serpent when he broke it as an idol.
Greek chalkos (G5475) — copper, brass, money; the sounding brass of 1 Corinthians 13:1.
Greek chalkolibanon (G5474) — fine brass, burnished as in a furnace; the feet of the glorified Christ.
usage: Of the type of Christ lifted up: when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived (Numbers 21:9).
Of a heaven shut in covenant judgment: thy heaven that is over thy head shall be brass (Deuteronomy 28:23).
Of loud religion without love: I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal (1 Corinthians 13:1).
scriptures: Numbers 21:9
And Moses made a serpent of brass, and put it upon a pole, and it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived.
Deuteronomy 28:23
And thy heaven that is over thy head shall be brass, and the earth that is under thee shall be iron.
1 Corinthians 13:1
Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.
Revelation 1:15
And his feet like unto fine brass, as if they burned in a furnace; and his voice as the sound of many waters.

pos: n. (a precious white metal; the metal of redemption money; rendering Hebrew keseph, Greek argurion)
etymology: From the Saxon seolfer. Hebrew keseph means both the metal and money itself, from a root meaning to long for or be pale — the same word serves for silver and for the price paid, which is why the ransom money of Exodus 30 is simply keseph.
biblical_def: Silver is the redemption metal. Every Israelite numbered in the census paid a half shekel of silver as atonement money for his soul, and that silver was melted into the sockets on which the tabernacle boards stood — the whole structure resting on redemption money. Silver is therefore the natural biblical figure for a price paid, and it carries the darkest transaction in Scripture: “And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver” (Matthew 26:15), the price of a gored slave under the law, offered for the Son of God. Silver is also the metal of refining, and Scripture uses it for God's work in his people: “I will bring the third part through the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined” (Zechariah 13:9). The refiner sits over the crucible and does not leave it, and the fire is measured, not arbitrary. The Psalter uses the same image for Scripture itself: “The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times” (Psalm 12:6). And Proverbs measures speech by it: “The tongue of the just is as choice silver” (Proverbs 10:20).
webster_summary: The redemption metal — atonement money in the census, and the sockets of the tabernacle. Also the metal of refining, used of God purifying his people and of the purity of his words.
webster_full: SILVER, n. [Sax. seolfer.] A metal of a white color and lively brilliancy, the most ductile after gold; in Scripture often put for money.
2. Money; coin made of silver; as, thirty pieces of silver, Matt. 26.
3. Anything of a pale white color, or resembling silver; as, silver hair.
4. The atonement money of the census, out of which the sockets of the tabernacle were cast, Exod. 30, 38.
5. In Scripture, a figure of refining; as, refine them as silver is refined, Zech. 13.
corruption_summary: Silver is read as wealth and nothing more, so the ransom logic behind it disappears. Scripture makes silver atonement money, and the price of Christ was counted out in it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What is commonly missed is a connection Scripture draws deliberately. The half shekel of Exodus 30 was called a ransom for the soul, identical for rich and poor, and the metal was cast into the foundation sockets of the tabernacle. Israel worshipped in a tent standing on redemption money, which is a sermon in silver: there is no approach to God that does not rest on a price paid, and the price is the same for every man.

The principle to recover follows into Matthew 26:15 and its terrible arithmetic. Thirty pieces of silver was the compensation fixed in Exodus 21 for a slave gored by an ox — the legal value of the least valuable life — and it was the figure at which the Son of God was valued by one who had walked with him three years. Zechariah had foretold the sum and the potter's field. Peter draws the conclusion the whole metal points to: ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ.
roots_summary: Hebrew keseph is both silver and money, so that a price and the metal share one word; tsaraph is to refine or smelt. Greek argurion is silver or a piece of money, and arguros the metal itself.
roots_lines: Hebrew keseph (H3701) — silver, money, price; the atonement money of the census.
Hebrew tsaraph (H6884) — to smelt, to refine, to test; the refiner of Malachi 3:3.
Hebrew kopher (H3724) — a ransom, a covering price; what the half shekel was called.
Greek argurion (G694) — silver, a piece of silver; the thirty pieces of Matthew 26:15.
Greek lutron (G3083) — a ransom; the Son of man came to give his life a ransom for many.
usage: Of the price set on Christ: they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:15).
Of God's measured refining of his people: I will refine them as silver is refined (Zechariah 13:9).
Of the purity of Scripture: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times (Psalm 12:6).
scriptures: Matthew 26:15
And said unto them, What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver.
Zechariah 13:9

And I will bring the third part through the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined, and will try them as gold is tried: they shall call on my name, and I will hear them: I will say, It is my people: and they shall say, The LORD is my God.
Psalm 12:6
The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times.
Proverbs 10:20
The tongue of the just is as choice silver: the heart of the wicked is little worth.

pos: n. (the most precious metal; the metal of the holy place; rendering Hebrew zahab, Greek chrusos)
etymology: From the Saxon gold, related to gelo, yellow. Hebrew zahab is from a root meaning to shimmer or be yellow, and it is the first metal named in Scripture — the gold of Havilah is called good in Genesis 2, before the fall and before any commerce in it.
biblical_def: Gold is the metal of the holy place. The ark, the mercy seat, the table, the candlestick, and the altar of incense are gold or overlaid with it, while the outer court is brass, so that the metals mark increasing nearness to God. “And thou shalt make a mercy seat of pure gold” (Exodus 25:17) — the place where the blood was sprinkled and where God promised to meet with Moses is the purest metal in the sanctuary. Scripture consistently ranks gold below things that cannot be mined. Proverbs sets character above it: “A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, and loving favour rather than silver and gold” (Proverbs 22:1). Peter sets faith above it: the trial of your faith is “much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire” (1 Peter 1:7) — gold perishes, and tested faith does not. Job, in the middle of unexplained suffering, makes gold the figure of what God is doing to him: “when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold” (Job 23:10). And the last vision reduces gold to paving: in the city, “the street of the city was pure gold, as it were transparent glass” (Revelation 21:21) — what men kill for is walked on there.
webster_summary: The most precious metal, and in the tabernacle the metal of the holy place and the mercy seat. Scripture consistently ranks a good name, tried faith, and the words of God above it.
webster_full: GOLD, n. [Sax. gold.] A precious metal of a bright yellow color, the most ductile and malleable of all metals, and of great weight.
2. Money; riches; wealth; as, the love of gold.
3. Something pleasing or valuable; as, a heart of gold.
4. In the tabernacle, the metal of the ark, the mercy seat, the table, and the candlestick.
5. In Scripture, a figure of tried faith; as, when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold, Job 23.
corruption_summary: Gold remains the standard of value, and Scripture agrees it is precious while insisting it perishes. The consistent biblical move is to name something better — a good name, tried faith, the words of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Two familiar errors attach to this metal. The first is the love of it, which Paul calls the root of all evil — not money itself, but the love of money, a distinction popular misquotation regularly loses. The second is the ascetic overcorrection that treats wealth as inherently sinful, which the tabernacle refutes: God commanded a great deal of gold for his sanctuary, and Abraham, Job, and Joseph of Arimathaea were wealthy men. Gold is a good creature; the question is always what a man does with it and what he thinks it can buy.

The principle to recover is the ranking Scripture keeps making. Proverbs 22:1 puts a good name above it, Psalm 19 puts the judgments of the LORD above much fine gold, and 1 Peter 1:7 puts tested faith above it on the specific ground that gold perishes and faith does not. Revelation 21:21 completes the argument with an image rather than a proposition: in the city gold is paving material. Nothing in Scripture despises gold, and nothing in Scripture is impressed by it.
roots_summary: Hebrew zahab is gold, from a root of shimmering; paz is fine or refined gold, and kethem is pure gold. Greek chrusos is gold and chrusion a golden article or coin.
roots_lines: Hebrew zahab (H2091) — gold; the metal of the ark, the mercy seat, and the holy place furniture.
Hebrew paz (H6337) — fine gold, refined gold; more to be desired than much fine gold, Psalm 19:10.
Hebrew kethem (H3800) — pure gold; used in Job and the Song for what is most precious.
Greek chrusos (G5557) — gold; the gift of the wise men and the paving of the city.
Greek chrusion (G5553) — a golden article, gold coin; I counsel thee to buy of me gold tried in the fire.
usage: Of the mercy seat where God met with Moses: thou shalt make a mercy seat of pure gold (Exodus 25:17).
Of tried faith ranked above it: much more precious than of gold that perisheth (1 Peter 1:7).
Of its final status in the city: the street of the city was pure gold (Revelation 21:21).
scriptures: Exodus 25:17
And thou shalt make a mercy seat of pure gold: two cubits and a half shall be the length thereof, and a cubit and a half the breadth thereof.
1 Peter 1:7
That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ:
But he knoweth the way that I take: when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold.
Revelation 21:21
And the twelve gates were twelve pearls; every several gate was of one pearl: and the street of the city was pure gold, as it were transparent glass.

pos: a. (made of or resembling gold; rendering Hebrew zahab in construct, Greek chruseos)
etymology: From gold with the Saxon adjectival ending -en, as in wooden and earthen — the ending denotes material, so golden means made of gold before it means merely excellent.
biblical_def: Golden as an adjective attaches chiefly to the furniture of worship, and the objects it names are among the richest types in Scripture. Hebrews lists the holiest's contents: it “had the golden censer, and the ark of the covenant overlaid round about with gold, wherein was the golden pot that had manna, and Aaron's rod that budded” (Hebrews 9:4). Zechariah is shown a golden lampstand fed by two olive trees — “behold a candlestick all of gold, with a bowl upon the top of it” (Zechariah 4:2) — and its lesson is given in the next breath: not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit. John's Revelation takes up the same figure and interprets it: “the seven candlesticks which thou sawest are the seven churches” (Revelation 1:20), so that the golden lampstand of the sanctuary becomes the church bearing light in the world, with Christ walking in the midst. The crowns of the elders are golden too, and what they do with them is the point: “four and twenty elders sitting, clothed in white raiment; and they had on their heads crowns of gold” (Revelation 4:4), crowns which they cast before the throne. Every golden thing in the heavenly vision ends up either bearing light or being laid down.
webster_summary: Made of gold. The adjective belongs to the furniture of worship — the golden censer, the golden pot of manna, the golden candlestick that becomes the church, and the crowns the elders cast down.
webster_full: GOLDEN, a. [from gold.] Made of gold; consisting of gold; as, a golden cup.
2. Bright; shining; resembling gold in color; as, golden hair.
3. Excellent; most valuable; as, the golden rule; a golden opportunity.
4. Happy; pre-eminently favorable; as, a golden age.
5. In Scripture, of the sanctuary furniture; as, the golden censer and the golden pot that had manna, Heb. 9.
corruption_summary: Golden has drifted to mean merely excellent — a golden opportunity, a golden age — and the material sense that governs its biblical use is lost. In Scripture the golden things are worship furniture, and every one of them points to Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The drift is metaphorical rather than doctrinal, but it costs the reader something. When golden means only excellent, the golden pot of manna in Hebrews 9:4 registers as a fine vessel rather than as a preserved portion of wilderness bread kept before God — the sustenance of a rebellious people memorialised in the holiest place, alongside the rod that budded and the tables of the covenant they had broken. The three items in the ark are three monuments to grace toward an unworthy nation.

The principle to recover is the interpretation Revelation supplies for the chief golden object. The seven golden candlesticks are the churches, which means a congregation is a lampstand: it does not generate light, it holds it up, and its business is to burn where it has been set. Zechariah 4:2 makes the fuel supply the whole lesson — the oil comes from the olive trees, not from the lamp — and the word to Zerubbabel follows, not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, saith the LORD of hosts. A church trying to shine by its own resources has mistaken itself for the oil.
roots_summary: Hebrew expresses the adjective by construct with zahab, gold, or by sagur, pure or shut-up gold. Greek chruseos is golden and luchnia is the lampstand rendered candlestick.
roots_lines: Hebrew zahab (H2091) — gold; Hebrew forms the adjective by construct rather than a separate word.
Hebrew menorah (H4501) — lampstand; the golden candlestick of the holy place and of Zechariah 4.
Greek chruseos (G5552) — golden, made of gold; used of the censer, the pot, and the candlesticks.
Greek luchnia (G3087) — lampstand, candlestick; interpreted as the churches in Revelation 1:20.
Greek stephanos (G4735) — a victor's crown; the golden crowns cast before the throne.
usage: Of the contents of the ark: the golden pot that had manna, and Aaron's rod that budded (Hebrews 9:4).
Of the lampstand fed by the Spirit: a candlestick all of gold, with a bowl upon the top of it (Zechariah 4:2).
Of the churches: the seven candlesticks which thou sawest are the seven churches (Revelation 1:20).
scriptures: Hebrews 9:4
Which had the golden censer, and the ark of the covenant overlaid round about with gold, wherein was the golden pot that had manna, and Aaron's rod that budded, and the tables of the covenant;
Zechariah 4:2

And said unto me, What seest thou? And I said, I have looked, and behold a candlestick all of gold, with a bowl upon the top of it, and his seven lamps thereon, and seven pipes to the seven lamps, which are upon the top thereof:
Revelation 1:20

The mystery of the seven stars which thou sawest in my right hand, and the seven golden candlesticks. The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches: and the seven candlesticks which thou sawest are the seven churches.
Revelation 4:4
And round about the throne were four and twenty seats: and upon the seats I saw four and twenty elders sitting, clothed in white raiment; and they had on their heads crowns of gold.

pos: a. (melted, cast from metal; rendering Hebrew massekah and mutsaq)
etymology: Old past participle of melt, from the Saxon meltan. Hebrew massekah means a poured or cast image, from nasak, to pour out — the same root as a drink offering poured to God, which makes the idolatrous casting a grim parody.
biblical_def: Molten describes metal melted and poured into a mould, and Scripture uses it in two directions that sit uncomfortably close together. Lawfully, it describes great works commanded for the worship of God: Solomon “made a molten sea, ten cubits from the one brim to the other” (1 Kings 7:23), the great laver in which the priests washed. Unlawfully, and far more often, it names the manufacture of idols. Aaron “fashioned it with a graving tool, after he had made it a molten calf” (Exodus 32:4), and the LORD's report of it to Moses on the mountain is blunt: “they have made them a molten image” (Deuteronomy 9:12). The sin at Sinai was not the worship of a rival god — Aaron proclaimed a feast to the LORD — but the worship of the true God by an image of Israel's own casting, which is the second commandment's exact concern. Isaiah exposes the absurdity of the trade: “The workman melteth a graven image, and the goldsmith spreadeth it over with gold” (Isaiah 40:19) — a god that must be manufactured, plated, and then fastened down so it will not topple. Habakkuk asks the question that ends the matter: what profiteth the molten image, a teacher of lies?
webster_summary: Melted and cast in a mould. Used of the molten sea Solomon made for the temple, and far more often of idols — the molten calf being worship of the true God by an image of Israel's own casting.
webster_full: MOLTEN, pp. of melt, an old participle. Melted; fused by heat.
2. Made of melted metal; cast in a mould; as, a molten image.
3. Of the great laver of the temple; as, he made a molten sea, 1 Kings 7.
4. In Scripture, of idolatry; as, they have made them a molten image, Deut. 9.
5. Figuratively, of the heart failing; as, the hearts of the people melted.
corruption_summary: Idolatry is imagined as a primitive matter of statues, safely behind us. The molten calf was an image of the true God made to Israel's specification, and that error is perennial.
corruption_paragraphs: The comfortable reading of Exodus 32 says Israel abandoned the LORD for a foreign deity, which lets a modern reader off. The text says otherwise: Aaron built an altar before the calf and proclaimed a feast to the LORD. The people were not swapping gods; they were worshipping the God who brought them out of Egypt by means of an image they had cast themselves, and the second commandment forbids exactly that. Idolatry in its most common biblical form is not the worship of another god but the worship of the true God in a way he has not commanded — which is why the regulative principle follows from this commandment and not merely from taste.

The principle to recover is Isaiah's mockery in 40:19, transposed to our own manufacture. A god who must be cast is a god shaped by the caster, and men still prefer a deity of their own specification — a God without wrath, or without particular election, or without the exclusivity of Christ — assembled from the attributes they find agreeable. That is a molten image with no metal in it. Habakkuk 2:18 gives the verdict: the molten image is a teacher of lies, precisely because the maker trusts in the work of his own hands.
roots_summary: Hebrew massekah is a cast image, from nasak, to pour out — the same root as a poured drink offering. Mutsaq means cast or hard-poured, and pesel is the carved image with which massekah is often paired.
roots_lines: Hebrew massekah (H4541) — a molten or cast image; the calf at Sinai and the calves at Dan and Bethel.
Hebrew nasak (H5258) — to pour out, to cast metal; also used of pouring a drink offering.
Hebrew mutsaq (H3332) — cast, poured, hardened; used of the molten sea in 1 Kings 7:23.
Hebrew pesel (H6459) — a graven image; frequently paired with massekah in the prophets.
Greek choneuo — to cast or found metal; the Septuagint's verb for making a molten image.
usage: Of a lawful work for the temple: he made a molten sea, ten cubits from the one brim to the other (1 Kings 7:23).
Of the sin at Sinai: after he had made it a molten calf (Exodus 32:4).
Of the manufacture of gods: the workman melteth a graven image, and the goldsmith spreadeth it over with gold (Isaiah 40:19).
scriptures: 1 Kings 7:23
And he made a molten sea, ten cubits from the one brim to the other: it was round all about, and his height was five cubits: and a line of thirty cubits did compass it round about.
Exodus 32:4

And he received them at their hand, and fashioned it with a graving tool, after he had made it a molten calf: and they said, These be thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt.
Deuteronomy 9:12

And the LORD said unto me, Arise, get thee down quickly from hence; for thy people which thou hast brought forth out of Egypt have corrupted themselves; they are quickly turned aside out of the way which I commanded them; they have made them a molten image.
Isaiah 40:19
The workman melteth a graven image, and the goldsmith spreadeth it over with gold, and casteth silver chains.

etymology: Past participle of grave, from the Saxon grafan, to dig or carve — the same root as grave, a dug place, and engrave. Hebrew pesel is from pasal, to hew or carve, and denotes an image cut from wood or stone as distinct from one cast from metal.
biblical_def: Graven means carved, and the phrase graven image stands at the head of the second commandment: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth” (Exodus 20:4). The commandment does not forbid art; it forbids the making of images for worship, and the reason given in Deuteronomy 4 is that Israel saw no similitude at Horeb but only heard a voice. God has appointed how he is to be approached, and the appointed means is his word. The Psalter pronounces on the practice without qualification: “Confounded be all they that serve graven images, that boast themselves of idols” (Psalm 97:7). Habakkuk exposes the logic: “What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it; the molten image, and a teacher of lies, that the maker of his work trusteth therein?” (Habakkuk 2:18) — the maker trusts what he has made, which is the whole absurdity in one sentence. And Isaiah gives God's own ground for the prohibition: “I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images” (Isaiah 42:8). The issue is not aesthetics but jealousy for glory.
webster_summary: Carved or engraved. The graven image of the second commandment is an image made for worship; God's stated ground for the prohibition is that he will not give his glory to another.
webster_full: GRAVEN, pp. of grave. [Sax. grafan, to dig, to carve.] Carved; cut with a chisel; engraved.
2. Impressed deeply; as, graven on the heart.
3. A graven image, an idol cut from wood or stone, as distinguished from a molten image cast from metal.
4. In Scripture, thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, Exod. 20.
5. Of the priestly stones; as, graven as signets, with the names of the children of Israel, Exod. 28.
corruption_summary: The second commandment is often read as forbidding art, or else quietly dropped as belonging to a superseded era. Its actual concern is that God be worshipped only as he has commanded, and its ground is his jealousy for his own glory.
corruption_paragraphs: Two misreadings compete. The iconoclastic overreach takes the commandment as a ban on representational art as such, which the text does not say and the tabernacle refutes — God commanded cherubim on the mercy seat, pomegranates on the hem, and oxen under the molten sea. The permissive reading goes the other way and treats images of Christ, or of God the Father, as aids to devotion rather than as breaches of the command. The Reformed confessions have not granted that distinction, holding that no image of God is lawful because no image can represent him and every attempt misrepresents him.

The principle to recover is the reason God himself gives in Isaiah 42:8: my glory will I not give to another. This is not divine touchiness but the only honest position for the one Being to whom glory actually belongs. Habakkuk 2:18 shows what is lost when the commandment is set aside — a man ends up trusting the work of his own hands and calls it faith. The commandment protects worship from the worshipper's imagination, which is exactly why every generation finds it inconvenient.
roots_summary: Hebrew pesel is a carved image, from pasal, to hew; chaqaq is to inscribe or engrave, used of writing on stone. Greek glupton renders pesel in the Septuagint, and eidolon is the general word for an idol.
roots_lines: Hebrew pesel (H6459) — a graven image, carved from wood or stone; the word of the second commandment.
Hebrew pasal (H6458) — to hew, to carve; also used of hewing the second tables of stone.
Hebrew chaqaq (H2710) — to inscribe, to engrave, to decree; graven on the palms of God's hands, Isaiah 49:16.
Hebrew pittuach (H6603) — an engraving; the priestly stones graven as signets.
Greek eidolon (G1497) — an image, an idol; keep yourselves from idols, 1 John 5:21.
usage: Of the second commandment: thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image (Exodus 20:4).
Of the folly of trusting one's own workmanship: the maker of his work trusteth therein (Habakkuk 2:18).
Of God's ground for the prohibition: my glory will I not give to another (Isaiah 42:8).
scriptures: Exodus 20:4
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
Psalm 97:7
Confounded be all they that serve graven images, that boast themselves of idols: worship him, all ye gods.
Habakkuk 2:18
What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it; the molten image, and a teacher of lies, that the maker of his work trusteth therein, to make dumb idols?
Isaiah 42:8

pos: n. and a. (a costly dye and the cloth dyed with it; rendering Hebrew argaman, Greek porphura)
etymology: From the Latin purpura, from the Greek porphura, the murex shellfish from which the dye was extracted — thousands of shellfish for a few grams, which is why purple meant wealth throughout the ancient world. Hebrew argaman denotes the reddish-purple of Tyrian manufacture.
biblical_def: Purple is the colour of royalty and of costliness, and Scripture puts it to three uses. It is a tabernacle colour, commanded with blue and scarlet for the curtains, the veil, and the priestly garments — the sanctuary was woven in the colours of a king's house. It is the mark of wealth, and our Lord uses it to set the scene of a parable without a word of comment: “There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day” (Luke 16:19), the man who ended in torment while Lazarus was carried by angels. Most piercingly, it is the colour of the mockery: “And they clothed him with purple, and platted a crown of thorns, and put it about his head” (Mark 15:17). The soldiers dressed him as a king in jest, and every article of the jest was true — the robe, the crown, the homage, the title over the cross. Scripture also records purple as an honest trade and the occasion of a conversion: “a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, which worshipped God, heard us” (Acts 16:14), and the Lord opened her heart, so that Europe's first recorded convert was a dealer in this dye.
webster_summary: A costly dye from the murex shellfish, hence the colour of royalty and wealth. A tabernacle colour, the rich man's clothing in the parable, and the robe in which soldiers mocked the true King.
webster_full: PURPLE, a. [L. purpura; Gr. porphura, the shellfish yielding the dye.] Designating a color composed of red and blue blended, much admired and anciently used by persons of rank.
2. As a noun, a purple color; also, a purple robe, the badge of royal or imperial dignity.
3. Dyed with blood; as, purple hands — a poetic use.
4. In the tabernacle, one of the three colors commanded for the curtains and priestly garments, with blue and scarlet.
5. In Scripture, of the mockery of Christ; they clothed him with purple, Mark 15.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Purple is now cheap, and a colour that once cost a fortune reads as ordinary — which flattens both the tabernacle's extravagance and the cruelty of the robe at the praetorium.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What synthetic dye has removed is the sense of cost. Purple once required thousands of murex shells for a small quantity, so a purple robe was a fortune worn; that is why it signalled rank and why Lydia's trade made her a woman of means able to house Paul's company. When the colour is cheap, Luke 16:19 loses its edge and the rich man merely seems well dressed rather than conspicuously and daily extravagant while a beggar lay at his gate.

The principle to recover is the terrible accuracy of Mark 15:17. The soldiers meant the purple as a joke and dressed him in the truth. He was a King; the robe was appropriate; the crown was the curse of Genesis 3 woven into a diadem; the homage they offered in scorn will one day be offered in earnest by every knee. And the tabernacle's purple points the same way, since the God who commanded the costly colours for a tent gave his Son to be mocked in a borrowed one.
roots_summary: Hebrew argaman is reddish-purple, the Tyrian dye; tekeleth is the blue-violet often named beside it. Greek porphura is the murex, the dye, and the robe, and porphuropolis is a seller of purple, Lydia's trade.

Hebrew tekeleth (H8504) — blue, violet; the companion colour to purple and scarlet.

Greek porphuropolis (G4211) — a seller of purple; the description of Lydia in Acts 16:14.

pos: a. and n. (the colour of the heavens; a tabernacle colour; rendering Hebrew tekeleth)
etymology: From the Old French bleu, of Germanic origin. Hebrew tekeleth is a blue-violet dye, also obtained from a shellfish, and is the colour most associated with heaven — the pavement under God's feet in Exodus 24 is like a sapphire stone, as it were the body of heaven in his clearness.
biblical_def: Blue is a commanded colour of the sanctuary, and Scripture gives it a specific office: it is the colour of remembrance and of heavenly things. The high priest's robe was made entirely of it — “And thou shalt make the robe of the ephod all of blue” (Exodus 28:31) — and the golden plate on his mitre, engraved HOLINESS TO THE LORD, was fastened with “a blue lace, that it may be upon the mitre” (Exodus 28:37). Blue also carried the law into the daily dress of every Israelite, not merely the priest's: God commanded that they “make them fringes in the borders of their garments… and that they put upon the fringe of the borders a ribband of blue” (Numbers 15:38), and the stated purpose was memory — that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the LORD, and do them. It is the thread of a wearable catechism. When the camp moved, the ark was covered first with the veil, then with badgers' skins, and then “a cloth wholly of blue” (Numbers 4:6) — the most sacred object in Israel travelling under the colour of heaven, so that the marching camp saw a patch of sky moving in its midst.
webster_summary: The blue-violet tekeleth of the sanctuary — the colour of the heavens. The high priest's robe was all of blue, and every Israelite wore a ribband of blue on his fringe to remember the commandments.
webster_full: BLUE, a. [Fr. bleu.] One of the seven primary colors, being that of the clear sky.
2. As a noun, the color itself; also, blue cloth or dye.
3. In the tabernacle, one of the three commanded colors, with purple and scarlet.
4. Of the high priest's robe, made wholly of blue, Exod. 28.
5. In Scripture, a ribband of blue upon the fringe, for remembrance of the commandments, Num. 15.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What has been lost is the deliberate use of the visible to serve memory — God appointing a thread of colour so that a man would look, remember, and obey.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The instructive thing about Numbers 15:38 is how ordinary the mechanism is. God knows that his people forget, and rather than merely commanding them not to, he attaches a blue thread to the hem of every garment so that the reminder is in the corner of the eye all day. The text gives the reason plainly: that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the LORD, and do them, and that ye seek not after your own heart and your own eyes.

The principle to recover is not a fringe on the coat — the ceremonial law is fulfilled in Christ and its shadows are not to be reinstituted. It is the recognition that God accommodates our weak memories, and that he has appointed means for the same end under the new covenant: the reading and preaching of the word, the Lord's Supper as a remembrance, the Lord's Day itself recurring every seventh day. Our Lord's rebuke of the Pharisees for enlarging their borders shows the abuse to avoid, where a means of remembrance becomes a badge of display; but the abuse does not cancel the wisdom of appointed reminders.
roots_summary: Hebrew tekeleth is blue-violet, a shellfish dye, and the sanctuary's heavenly colour; tsitsith is the fringe to which the blue ribband was fastened. Greek huakinthinos renders it in the Septuagint.

pos: n. (wood prepared for building; rendering Hebrew ets and aeh)
etymology: From the Saxon timbrian, to build — timber is literally building-stuff, and the same root gives German Zimmer, a room. Hebrew ets is the general word for tree or wood, so that the Hebrew reader hears tree where the English hears timber.
biblical_def: Timber is wood prepared for building, and Scripture treats it soberly as material, with two memorable exceptions where the timber speaks. Ezra records the resumption of the temple work in the flat prose of an official report: “this work goeth fast on, and prospereth in their hands” — the enquiry noting that great stones were laid in the walls and “timber is laid in the walls” (Ezra 5:8). The building of God's house is a matter of hauling and joinery as much as of vision, and Scripture does not despise the ledger. But Habakkuk turns the material into a witness against injustice: “For the stone shall cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the timber shall answer it” (Habakkuk 2:11) — a house built with the wages of oppression will testify against its builder from its own fabric, which is among the most arresting figures in the prophets. Zechariah presses the same logic to its end in the vision of the flying roll, where the curse enters the house of the thief and the false swearer and “shall consume it with the timber thereof and the stones thereof” (Zechariah 5:4). What was gained by fraud is not merely taken away; it is consumed down to the frame.
webster_summary: Wood prepared for building — the word is literally building-stuff. Scripture records it in the temple accounts, and twice makes it a witness: the beam out of the timber answers the crying stone.
webster_full: TIMBER, n. [Sax. timbrian, to build.] That sort of wood which is proper for buildings or for tools, utensils, vessels and the like.
2. The body or stem of a tree suitable for building.
3. Material in general; as, the timber of a man's character — a figurative use.
4. In shipbuilding, a rib or curving piece of wood branching outward from the keel.
5. In Scripture, timber is laid in the walls, Ezra 5; the beam out of the timber shall answer it, Hab. 2.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is plain; what is easily missed is Habakkuk's doctrine that a house built by oppression testifies against its builder out of its own beams.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Timber is an ordinary building word and remains one. Its interest lies in what the prophets do with it. Habakkuk 2:11 is addressed to a man who buildeth a town with blood and establisheth a city by iniquity, and the sentence pronounced is not that the house will be seized but that the house will speak. Wealth gained by defrauding labourers does not become neutral once it is converted into property; James says the same of hire kept back by fraud, which crieth, and the cries have entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth.

The principle to recover is that God attends to how a thing was built and not only to what was built. Ezra 5:8 shows the other side and is worth holding beside it: the temple went up by ordinary means, timber laid in walls, and the eye of God was upon the elders of the Jews so that the work prospered. A congregation is right to keep accounts carefully and to build honestly, because the materials of a house raised by oppression will one day give evidence, and Zechariah 5:4 says the curse consumes the timber thereof and the stones thereof.
roots_summary: Hebrew ets is tree or wood, the general term, and in Ezra's Aramaic aeh serves the same purpose; qorah is a beam or rafter. Greek xulon is wood or timber, and is also the word for the tree on which Christ hung.

pos: n. (ground meal, especially the finest; the substance of the meat offering; rendering Hebrew soleth)
etymology: From the French fleur, the flower of the meal — the finest part sifted out, as one speaks of the flower of an army. Hebrew soleth denotes fine flour specifically, distinguished from qemach, ordinary meal.
biblical_def: Flour is the substance of the meat offering, which the Authorized Version so names using meat in its old sense of food generally — it is a grain offering, and no flesh is in it. The law prescribes it: “when any will offer a meat offering unto the LORD, his offering shall be of fine flour; and he shall pour oil upon it, and put frankincense thereon” (Leviticus 2:1). Fine flour is required, not coarse meal — the best of the harvest, sifted — and the daily burnt offering was accompanied by “a tenth part of an ephah of flour for a meat offering, mingled with the fourth part of an hin of beaten oil” (Numbers 28:5), morning and evening without fail. The typology is rich and restrained. The grain offering is the only offering without blood, presented after the burnt offering: having been accepted through sacrifice, the worshipper then offers the fruit of his labour and the substance of his table. Its evenness is part of the meaning, for flour is grain crushed until no grain is distinguishable from another — a fit figure of the perfect, even humanity of Christ, in whom no quality outran another. The cleansed leper's restoration required it too: with the lambs, “three tenth deals of fine flour for a meat offering” (Leviticus 14:10).
webster_summary: The finest ground meal — the flower of the wheat. The substance of the meat offering, the one bloodless offering, presented with oil and frankincense after the burnt offering had been accepted.
webster_full: FLOUR, n. [Fr. fleur, the flower or finest part.] The edible part of corn; meal finely ground and bolted, freed from the bran.
2. The fine parts of any substance reduced to powder.
3. In Scripture, fine flour, the substance of the meat offering, Lev. 2.
4. Offered with oil and frankincense, and a portion burnt as a memorial upon the altar.
5. Required in the cleansing of the leper and in the daily continual offering, Lev. 14, Num. 28.
corruption_summary: The grain offering is skipped as ritual detail, and with it goes the pattern it teaches: worship of the whole life — labour, bread, and table — presented only after atonement has been accepted.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Leviticus 2 is among the least read chapters in Scripture, and the loss is real. The meat offering follows the burnt offering in the order of the chapters, and the sequence is the doctrine: the burnt offering deals with the worshipper's acceptance through a substitute, and only then does he bring the produce of his own hands. A man cannot offer his work to God as the ground of his standing; he offers it as the fruit of a standing already secured. Every attempt to reverse that order is a return to Cain, who brought of the fruit of the ground with no lamb before it.

The principle to recover is that the ordinary is offerable. Flour, oil, and frankincense are kitchen things, and God appointed them a place on the altar alongside blood. Romans makes the same point in New Testament terms, urging believers to present their bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is their reasonable service. The fineness required — soleth, not coarse meal — forbids offering God the leavings, and the evenness of the flour, with no grain standing out from another, has long been taken by Reformed writers as a figure of the balanced perfection of Christ's human nature.
roots_summary: Hebrew soleth is fine flour, distinguished from qemach, common meal; minchah is the gift or meat offering it composes. Greek semidalis is the Septuagint's fine flour, appearing in the merchandise of Babylon.
